qAndA.question: What is the name of the galaxy cluster that Hubble used for this Frontier Field image?

qAndA.answer: Gravitational lensing, where the gravity of a massive object bends the light from objects behind it.
qAndA.question: What causes the "distortion effect" on the background galaxies in the Hubble image?
How far away is the small orange dot galaxy that is mentioned?

qAndA.answer: The video shows that the orange dot galaxy appears multiple times in the image because its light is being bent and magnified by the gravity of the foreground galaxy cluster.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: You may be familiar with Hubble's iconic deep field images, where Hubble peered farther
back into space and time than ever before, and you may have thought surely that's as
good as it gets.
But, a lot of Hubble scientists, inspired by Star Trek, want to continue boldly pushing
as far into the final frontier as we can.
So in celebration of Star Trek's new movie and the franchise's 50th anniversary, Hubble
is releasing its latest Frontier Field Image.
This image uses a clever trick from nature predicted by Einstein's general theory of
relativity called gravitational lensing to magnify distant galaxies that we may not
otherwise be able to see.
We point the telescope at a cluster of galaxies where there's so much mass that it's
warping the fabric of space time.
Light from behind the massive objects appears to bend around the cluster and we see this
incredible distortion effect on the appearance of the background galaxies.
In this image, the foreground galaxy cluster ABLE S1063 is about 4 billion light years
away.
You can see bright blue galaxies behind the cluster appearing as these stretched out arcs
and some even appear in multiple locations.
These galaxies are about twice as far away as the foreground cluster on the order of 8
billion light years.
Then, if you look at this small orange dot, that's an extremely distant galaxy we're seeing
nearly 13 billion light years away.
And here and here and here, that's actually all the same galaxy.
At 26 years in counting of cutting edge science, the Hubble Space Telescope continues to live
long and prosper.
